name: Microdermabrasion / HydraFacial

lead: Microdermabrasion and HydraFacial are light exfoliating facials that leave skin looking smoother, brighter and fresher straight after the session, which is why they are popular before events.

Microdermabrasion removes the outermost dead cells with crystals or a diamond tip plus suction. HydraFacial, also called hydradermabrasion, adds cleansing, suction-based extraction and serum application. Wikipedia notes results are temporary because skin renews roughly every 30 days, and authors of a 2024 imaging study state that clinical validation of HydraFacial efficacy is scarce.

paras: Sessions are done in clinics or salons without anaesthetic and are usually repeated every 2 to 4 weeks to keep the effect. They are often booked as a routine facial rather than a one-off.
Reported effects are usually minor: dryness, sun sensitivity and, rarely, bruising. Crystal-based systems raise inhalation and eye concerns, so eye protection is part of the process.

angle.text: Microdermabrasion and HydraFacial strip away surface dead cells, so skin looks smoother, brighter and fresher right after the session. Results are temporary, so sessions are repeated. Published efficacy data are sparse.

lead: Microdermabrasion is a non-invasive exfoliation that removes the outermost dead skin cells with crystals or a diamond tip combined with suction, usually without anaesthetic.[1] HydraFacial, also called hydradermabrasion, is a branded exfoliative facial that combines cleansing and peeling with suction-based extraction and serum application.[2][3]

Wikipedia notes results are temporary, since skin renews roughly every 30 days, so sessions are usually repeated every 2 to 4 weeks.[1] Authors of a 2024 imaging study state that clinical validation of HydraFacial efficacy is scarce.[2]

paras: The first microdermabrasion unit was developed in Italy in 1985 using aluminium oxide crystals. The FDA issued its first approval letter for such machines in 1996, the first US machine sold in January 1997, a diamond tip appeared in 1999, a bristle tip in 2005 and a crystal-free vacuum system in 2012.[1]

A 2024 study used line-field confocal optical coherence tomography to image skin changes after hydradermabrasion, noting that non-invasive histological validation had been scarce.[2] A 12-week open-label study of 20 adults with mild-to-moderate acne tested six HydraFacial Clarifying treatments, one every two weeks.[3] Registered trials include a 27-person study of three HydraFacial treatments on skin quality and hydration, and trials of a scalp version in hair thinning (44 participants completed; one not yet recruiting).[4][5][6] Wikipedia also cites a 2003 controlled assessment of microdermabrasion for damaged skin.[1] The sources reviewed here do not give effect sizes.
Wikipedia lists temporary dryness and sun sensitivity, and rarely bruising or scratches. Crystal-based systems carry concerns about inhalation and eye injury.[1]
